segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And you were dead in your offenses and sins,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the domain of the air, of the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Among them we too all once lived in the desires of our flesh, carrying out the wishes of the flesh and of the mind, and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: even when we were dead in our offenses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that in the coming ages he might display the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not from works, so that no one may boast.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are his handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore remember that once you, the Gentiles in the flesh, who are called the uncircumcision by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that at that time you were apart from Christ, shut out from citizenship in Israel and foreigners to the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the barrier of the dividing wall, the hostility, in his flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nullifying the law of commandments expressed in decrees, so that in himself he might create the two into one new person, making peace,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and might reconcile both to God in one body through the cross, killing the hostility by it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he came and announced the good news of peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, you are no longer foreigners and resident aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the holy ones and members of God’s household,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in whom you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.

notes.note: The Greek word means an age or era; older versions paraphrased it as 'course' and several modern ones as 'ways'. The phrase joins two expressions usually found separately, 'this age' and 'this world', to describe the present order of things. A minority of scholars read it as a personal power, 'the Aeon of this world', parallel to the ruler named next; most do not.

The air, the region between the earth and the heavens, was widely thought in antiquity to be the home of spirits. The word traditionally rendered 'power' means authority, and here the sphere in which authority is exercised, hence 'domain'. The ruler is not named, but readers have consistently understood the devil to be meant.

'Spirit' is in the genitive case, so by strict grammar it depends on 'ruler' (the ruler of the spirit) or stands in parallel with 'domain' or 'air'. Most English versions write 'the spirit', identifying it with the ruler himself, which gives a smoother sense but is not what the grammar most naturally says. The translation keeps the genitive; the question is disputed, and on either reading one hostile power is in view.

'This' is neuter in Greek, while 'grace' and 'faith' are both feminine nouns, so it most naturally refers to the whole fact of being saved by grace through faith. That is the majority scholarly view. A long-standing alternative takes 'this' to be faith specifically, making faith itself the gift.

The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations', and in the plural in Jewish usage it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant. It is one word in Greek.

notes.phrase: made in the flesh by hands
notes.traditional: made in the flesh by hands
notes.note: 'Made by hands' is a pointed word. In the Greek Old Testament it is a regular term for idols, and elsewhere in the New Testament it describes temples and other things of merely human construction. Using it of circumcision presents the labels 'circumcision' and 'uncircumcision' as distinctions at the level of the body.

notes.phrase: the barrier of the dividing wall
notes.note: Literally 'the dividing wall of the fence'. Many readers see an allusion to the stone barrier in the Jerusalem temple beyond which Gentiles were forbidden to go on pain of death, known from Josephus and from surviving warning inscriptions. Others think of the law itself, which Jewish writers of the period could describe as a fence around Israel. The reference is uncertain, and the two ideas are not exclusive.

The Greek syntax across verses 14–15 is disputed. 'The hostility' may explain what the dividing wall is (as here), or it may be the object of 'nullifying' together with the law: 'having nullified in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments'. Likewise 'in his flesh' can go with breaking down the wall or with nullifying the law. The translation keeps the Greek order so that both connections remain possible.

The Greek word means a human being, not specifically a male. Some modern versions use 'one new humanity', which is the point, but the image is of a single figure created in Christ out of two groups. 'Person' keeps that image.

'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek word is used for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

The word comes from the Greek version of Isaiah 28:16, where it is a stone laid in a foundation. Most scholars take it here as the cornerstone from which a building's lines are set. Some argue for the capstone or keystone that completes the structure at the top; the evidence for that sense is later and the question remains open.

The best-attested Greek text has no article, which in strict grammar would mean 'every building', as though several structures were growing into one temple. Most scholars and translations read 'the whole building', since Greek of this period uses the form loosely and the context describes a single structure. Some manuscripts add the article, making that sense explicit.

candidates.reason: Recurs across Paul and the Gospels; versions vary between trespasses, transgressions, offenses and sins, and it needs to be kept distinct from παράβασις and ἁμαρτία.

A key Pauline verb variously rendered abolish, nullify, set aside or bring to nothing; whether the law is 'abolished' or 'nullified' matters and should not vary between Romans, Corinthians, Galatians and Ephesians.
The Semitic 'walk' for conduct of life is frequent in the letters; translators split between 'walk' and 'live', and the choice should be uniform.
